Lessons.Title: Notice and Wonder
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U08:L14 is a STUDENT-DESIGNED Notice and Wonder instructional routine. It cannot be made source-faithful by substituting a predetermined number quiz for collecting classmates' perceptions, presenting images and recording questions.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Sharing Bread uses a source credited photograph by Couleur/Pixabay to prompt fraction interpretation of how a quantity is shared. Actual source image pixels and license terms are not silently reconstructed from text.

Activity1 Design Your Notice and Wonder: learner FINDS an image about sharing or interpreting a fraction as a quotient and writes POSSIBLE notices and wonders; participants select their own authentic image and justify why it will elicit mathematical thought.

Activity2 Facilitate Your Notice and Wonder: learner displays chosen image, poses both Notice/Wonder prompts, gives peer quiet think/discussion time, has classmates share and RECORDS their real observations. Teacher checks original delivery, accuracy and respectful facilitation.

Activity3 Design Your Notice and Wonder Part2: choose a NEW image about ANY mathematics learned during the year and predict what students notice/wonder. Gated original photo, learner artifact, peer interaction and end reflection require teacher review; selected digital cases check only original PROCEDURAL rules.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: the LEARNER creates a mathematical Notice and Wonder using an image, object or drawing they select, first emphasizing division-as-fractions and then an optional mathematics topic from the full Grade 5 course. The original source requires learners to FACILITATE their own task with classmates and record authentic observations. It is not a textbook image-identification quiz.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — design a fraction-sharing prompt: select a permission-appropriate photo or make an original drawing of five identical paper strips being shared equally among three learners. Ask peers 'What do you notice?' and 'What do you wonder?' The teacher might see observations about equal shares and a question about how much each learner receives; there is no mandated exact transcript. Five shared strips divided among three yields5/3=1 2/3 strips per learner, but computing the quotient is NOT the same as collecting classmates' questions.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — facilitate: show the learner-chosen image to another group, give quiet observation time, invite students' own notices and wonders, and record them without filling them in beforehand. Later discuss how a question such as 'what part belongs to one person?' might connect sharing to fraction notation. Teacher reviews whether actual peer voices are captured and whether the image/diagram depicts equal shares.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 3 — independent chosen topic: choose an original coordinate plane, a multiplication array, a volume model, or a real class observation (without personal data), then build another Notice and Wonder that genuinely invites curiosity. The mathematical content is intentionally unspecified by the 2021 source and must not be overwritten with a canned fixed problem.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Acceptance rubric: teacher checks media permission/provenance; representational accuracy; two distinct plausible open observations and questions; original learner selection; actual facilitation/recording; respectful discussion; and mathematical follow-up. A sample quotient check cannot automatically mark the student-created activity complete.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sharing as a fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: If a equal-size items are shared equally among b positive recipients, each gets a/b items.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 5 strips shared by3 people means5/3 strips per person.
KeyConcepts.Example: The source's aim is noticing and wondering about sharing, not mandatory single numeric output.

KeyConcepts.Title: A notice is an observation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An observation describes something visible or measurable without assuming a particular answer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 'There are five equal strips and three recipients' is a sample notice.
KeyConcepts.Example: Actual pupils' observations must be recorded as they occur.

KeyConcepts.Title: A wonder is a mathematical question
KeyConcepts.Definition: A useful question invites investigation and may have several valid forms.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 'Can the strips be cut into thirds with equal portions?' is a sample wonder.
KeyConcepts.Example: The learner designs and runs the discussion.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Use self-created drawings or permission-verified assets.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Fabricate learner-selected images, peer responses or exact source figure geometry as a precomputed single-answer item.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep source student-generated tasks as teacher-scored and use bounded source question families only for procedural rules or fixed expressions.

Teacher rubric assesses mathematical relevance, facilitation and actual recorded discussion.

Optional prior: Sharing-as-division can be written as a fraction, but it is one possible mathematical follow-up.
Optional prior: Teacher judgment is required for media, task design, facilitation and peer recording.

Lessons.Title: Estimation Exploration
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: the learner CREATES and FACILITATES an estimation task based on objects, an original drawing or a permitted image, specifically selecting a scenario where multi-digit multiplication is helpful. The original source asks students to propose too-low, plausible and too-high estimates and gather classmates' estimates; these are not predetermined exact-answer cards.

Activity 1 — original exemplar setup: draw a shelf with24 trays, each containing approximately18 small objects. Without announcing the tray count at first, invite peers to identify relevant quantities, the grouping structure and reasonable rough estimates. As an independent reference calculation,24×18=432 objects if all trays are full. That number is a model for the exemplar, not a count of a particular pupil's real object collection.

Activity 2 — design estimates: use200 objects as a deliberately low reference estimate, roughly430 as a plausible approximation, and700 as a deliberately high estimate under the hypothetical24×18 model. Explain why these are judged RELATIVE to the declared scenario rather than universal 'too low' values for any photograph. Better rounding can give20×20≈400, supporting the plausible range.

Activity 3 — facilitate: display the student's selected image or classroom arrangement, solicit individual estimates before revealing any counts, allow partner discussion, record classmates' actual too-low/about-right/too-high suggestions, and revise the estimate after seeing more detail. Students should justify how a structure of repeated equal groups supports multiplication; teacher evaluates if the estimates are truly reasoned.

Acceptance rubric: require learner-created or permission-verified image/object, a measurable repeated-group quantity, low/middle/high estimate with justification, actual peer-recorded estimates and facilitation. The software can check24×18 only as an exemplar numeric subskill; must not invent an actual classroom observation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate grouped totals
KeyConcepts.Definition: Repeated equal groups can be approximated with a multiplication product.
KeyConcepts.Example: A source image requires its own observed counts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use friendly factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: Round factors to estimate an order of magnitude before checking the exact product.
KeyConcepts.Example: Too-low and too-high need scenario-dependent reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Student-led estimation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid Estimation Exploration includes an introduced visual, estimates, discussion and refinement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Prompt peers before revealing the actual model counts.
KeyConcepts.Example: Record real suggestions, not scripted responses.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create a sample visual estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: A fictional original drawing shows24 groups of18 counters each.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Choose20×20≈400 as a quick benchmark.
Multiply24×18 using20×18+4×18.
Compare exact432 with the estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Defend estimate ranges
WorkedExamples.Question: Why could200,430 and700 be low/about right/high for the same drawn24×18 group model?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Observe that24×18=432.
Compare each candidate with432.
Explain that rough estimates depend on whether a full tray count was visible.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 200 low,430 near,700 high for this example.
WorkedExamples.Check: These thresholds are not universal or learner-provided evidence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Facilitation check
WorkedExamples.Question: What is needed beyond the exact product to finish the task?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Document original or rights-cleared image/objects.
Record peer estimates in their own words.
Explain how the estimate was revised after viewing more detail.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Teacher-scored original activity with real classroom evidence.
WorkedExamples.Check: A prefilled example number is never an automatic pass.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a correct product as evidence that students led an exploration
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 activity is to design and facilitate an estimate task.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an assessment rubric covering original design, group participation and reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Represent a rough estimate as an exact measured count
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Estimation often uses approximate source quantities or incomplete visuals.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label approximations and source counts separately.

SummaryPoints: The learner creates a visual estimation problem, not just computes an existing product.
Too-low/about-right/too-high answers are relative to the chosen source quantities.
Teacher validates authentic classroom participation, justification and asset permission.

Lessons.Title: Number Talk PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: the learner DESIGNS one or more Number Talk sequences to help classmates reason about dividing whole numbers by two-digit divisors using connections among expressions. The official 2021 task intentionally leaves multiple blanks for pupil-authored questions; any fixed list of answers can only be an exemplar, not the mandated completion.

Activity 1 — sample continuation: original sequence 40÷20=2,60÷20=3,400÷20=20 can be followed by420÷20=21. Explain how400÷20 and20÷20 combine to make420÷20 rather than presenting unrelated computations. An acceptable alternative might emphasize factor-of-ten scaling or another quotient relationship.

Activity 2 — design a second number talk: start with 240÷24=10 and72÷24=3; add 312÷24=13 and480÷24=20. Invite learners to describe how combining ten and three groups or doubling a known quotient creates convenient values. The original source accepts multiple choices; ask the learner to explain what their sequence teaches, then facilitate the discussion with a small group.

Activity 3 — extended source-like example: start 510÷51=10, then add102÷51=2,612÷51=12,714÷51=14. The selected expressions keep the same divisor and create useful patterns. Ask classmates to anticipate the quotient BEFORE computation, and document what they actually notice. Do not invent peers' responses.

Assessment: the teacher checks logical sequencing, at least one usable division strategy, each nonzero divisor, explanation of relationships, and student-led presentation/discussion. Numeric quotient checks are not complete source-task acceptance.

KeyConcepts.Title: Related division expressions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Known multiples of a divisor support new quotient computations.
KeyConcepts.Example: Useful Number Talks connect rather than merely list expressions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive sharing over sums
KeyConcepts.Definition: When the same nonzero divisor is used, (a+b)/d=a/d+b/d.
KeyConcepts.Example: This is a useful reasoned sequence pattern.

KeyConcepts.Title: Student-generated discussion
KeyConcepts.Definition: The source requires learner-created missing expressions and explanations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete a connected sequence
WorkedExamples.Question: Given40÷20,60÷20,400÷20, propose a meaningful next expression.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Observe that400÷20=20.
Notice that20÷20=1.
Combine400 and20 as a meaningful extension.
WorkedExamples.Check: Several other continuations may be valid.

WorkedExamples.Title: Combine known quotients
WorkedExamples.Question: Why is312÷24=13?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Decompose312 into240+72.
Divide both by24:10+3.
Add the partial quotients.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build an extension
WorkedExamples.Question: Add another related expression after510÷51=10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Identify51×2=102.
Add102 to510 to obtain612.
Predict the new quotient by adding2 to10.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Fill blanks with arbitrary unrelated expressions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The mathematical purpose is reasoning from known divisions and patterns.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain the mathematical relation linking proposed problems.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume one published answer uniquely completes an open Number Talk
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Many sequences can develop a valid strategy.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher reviews an original sequence and why its progression helps classmates.

SummaryPoints: Divide multi-digit numbers using related multiples and additive quotient reasoning.
A Number Talk design must be mathematically coherent and genuinely authored by the learner.
Teacher verifies facilitation and explanation; an automatically checked quotient is partial.

Lessons.Title: True or False?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: the learner DESIGNS true/false fraction addition and subtraction equations, first by adding one equation to a short set, then adding two, and finally creating a complete set of three. The source uses unlike denominators; evaluating correctness and explaining the resulting mathematical contrasts matter more than matching one authored example.

Warm-up: 5/6−4/9 converts to15/18−8/18=7/18. Compare with15/36, which is5/12 and not equal to7/18. A correct source-like True/False task may deliberately include a false equality so classmates must reason why the two sides differ.

Activity 1 — complete a sample set: design an additional statement that is either clearly TRUE by a valid common denominator, such as5/6−4/9=21/54, or FALSE in a meaningful way, such as5/6−4/9=1/2. Explain the equivalence 21/54=7/18 and why 1/2 exceeds the true difference. Multiple candidate equations are educationally valid if labeled correctly and accompanied by justification.

Activity 2 — mixed true/false items: with 4/7+3/7=1, design4/7+3/7=7/7 (true) and4/7+3/7=7/14 (false), then explain what changed. For a more challenging subtraction design, compare3/4−1/6=7/12 with3/4−1/6=2/10 (false); critique denominator addition and wrong equal-part units.

Activity 3 — facilitation: choose a coherent progression of three original equations; solicit classmates' reasons before revealing truth labels, then revise ambiguous statements. Teacher reviews the quality of intentionally false examples, accurate rationales and real peer discussion, not simply a list of truth values.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractional units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Unlike denominators must be converted to a common unit before adding or subtracting.

KeyConcepts.Title: A false equality is a teachable object
KeyConcepts.Definition: A plausible but incorrect fraction equality helps uncover a specific misconception.
KeyConcepts.Example: Adding fractions with equal denominators keeps the denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Teacher-designed task rationale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each created equality should have a verifiable truth value and an intended misconception or structure to discuss.
KeyConcepts.Example: The pupil should state why peers might initially disagree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Verify a source-like equality
WorkedExamples.Question: Is5/6−4/9=21/54 correct?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Find a common denominator18:15/18−8/18=7/18.
Simplify21/54 by three to7/18.
Compare the fractions.
WorkedExamples.Check: The same quantity has equivalent denominators.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create a meaningful false statement
WorkedExamples.Question: Is4/7+3/7=7/14 correct?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Recognize both fractions already have denominator7.
Add numerators to obtain7/7=1.
Compare7/14=1/2 with1.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher assesses whether the learner explains the denominator misconception.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique a mixed denominator difference
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate3/4−1/6=2/10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Find common denominator12.
Rewrite3/4 as9/12 and1/6 as2/12.
Subtract to obtain7/12 and compare to1/5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews rationales and original student-designed items.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add denominators when combining fraction units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The two denominators identify the SIZE of each part, not a tally to add.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert to equal-sized fraction parts first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a list of prewritten true/false checks as proof of student-designed facilitation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks the learner to develop and present their own items.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep exemplars separate from learner-authored three-equation set and class discussion.

SummaryPoints: Fraction-equation design should include verifiable true and/or purposefully false statements.
Common denominators justify correct values and expose misconceptions.
Creation, sequencing and facilitation are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Which One Doesn’t Belong?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: create and FACILITATE a Which One Doesn't Belong discussion using 3D volume shapes and later a mathematical topic of the learner's choice. The original source starts with a deck of three-dimensional shape cards and progressively moves from adding one original shape, to adding two, to designing all four. A task can support multiple reasonable outlier arguments; one automatically forced answer is inappropriate.

Activity 1 — first-party four-prism set: A is a2×2×2 cube (volume8), B is a1×2×4 rectangular prism (volume8), C is a2×2×3 prism (volume12), and D is a3×3×3 cube (volume27). Learners draw or construct the models and name shape attributes. A valid discussion may say B has three distinct edge lengths, C has exactly two equal edge lengths, or D has the largest volume. Several can be defended as not belonging based on specified criteria.

Activity 2 — design additional shapes and criteria: start with two unit-cube arrays (for example3×3×3 and2×2×3) and create two new arrays to emphasize either shared volume with different dimensions or a cube-versus-noncube classification. Ask classmates for different reasons why one array doesn't belong, and check whether each proposed feature is mathematically true. An attractive picture alone is not evidence of correct volume.

Activity 3 — learner's own topic: create a WODB about fraction equivalence, coordinate points, decimal representations, or other Grade 5 mathematics, and explain the pattern that makes each option potentially different. Invite peers to propose alternatives and respectfully justify them with mathematical properties rather than aesthetic judgments.

Acceptance rubric: mathematical accuracy of all four options, defensible reasons for multiple outliers, learner-created drawings or legally usable cards, meaningful peer feedback and actual facilitation all require teacher assessment. No fixed numeric key can substitute for the original open task.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume for rectangular arrays
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rectangular-prism array with edge lengths a,b,c has abc unit-cube volume.
KeyConcepts.Example: Equal volume can coexist with unequal edge lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Classify special shapes
KeyConcepts.Definition: A cube has three equal mutually perpendicular edge lengths; general prisms need not.
KeyConcepts.Example: Distinctions should use genuine shape properties.

KeyConcepts.Title: Defensible outlier criteria
KeyConcepts.Definition: A WODB argument identifies one mathematically accurate feature that distinguishes a selected option.
KeyConcepts.Rule: B alone has all three edge lengths distinct in the example.
KeyConcepts.Example: Other possible choices may also have defensible reasons.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two equal-volume shapes
WorkedExamples.Question: Do2×2×2 and1×2×4 have the same volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Multiply all three edges for each prism.
Obtain8 unit cubes for each.
Explain why different dimensions do not force different volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify a distinctive prism
WorkedExamples.Question: Among2×2×2,1×2×4,2×2×3,3×3×3, which uniquely has three different edge lengths?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: List each model's three edge lengths.
Check equality of the listed lengths.
Choose only the one with three distinct lengths.
WorkedExamples.Check: The source allows other correct WODB criteria.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain a separate outlier
WorkedExamples.Question: Which model in the set has the largest volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent exemplar and task rubric, NOT evidence a pupil has created or facilitated an original classroom task.
Steps: Compute8,8,12,27 cubic units.
Compare the four volumes.
Present a reasoned outlier claim.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the stated selection criterion and peer discussion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume WODB has exactly one objectively correct outlier
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The routine invites several mathematical classifications and arguments.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept justified alternative selections based on accurate attributes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Select volume from a shape's flat area alone
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count unit cube layers or multiply length×width×height.

SummaryPoints: A student-created WODB needs four mathematically valid and discussable representations.
Equal volume doesn't imply equal shape and outliers depend on stated properties.
Teacher reviews student drawings, choice of evidence and facilitation.
